newsitem.title: JAPAN: Copper trader Hamanaka feared Sumitomo dismissal.
newsitem.headline: Copper trader Hamanaka feared Sumitomo dismissal.

text.p: Yasuo Hamanaka, the former star trader who once dominated world copper markets, said at his trial on Wednesday that fear of dismissal made him hide mammoth trading losses in the late 1980s.

According to Tokyo prosecutors, Hamanaka and his former boss at Sumitomo Corp, Saburo Shimizu, began unauthorised trading in London Metal Exchange futures in 1985 to sustain the copper division's profitability after it recorded its first full-year profit in 10 years.

But the team instead incurred trading losses, which the two hid through off-the-book deals. By the time Shimizu quit the company in 1987 and Hamanaka took over as Sumitomo's copper team leader, their losses had climbed to 6.5 billion yen ($57.5 million).
"When Mr Shimizu resigned from the company, he was so exhausted and had lost his energy to keep trading. I had no choice but to take over the losses," Hamanaka told a Tokyo court.
"If I had confessed to the losses to the management then, I would have been demoted or dismissed," he said.
Hamanaka also said that Sumitomo's copper team was in the red in the 1970s, as Japanese end-users of copper had tried to pressure trading houses to lower their commission fees.
"Increasing profit margins and business opportunities were the top priorities of Sumitomo at the time, and I tried to live up to the company's expectation," he said.
Until he was fired in June 1996, Hamanaka was nicknamed "Mr Five Percent" and "Mr Copper" for his influence in the global copper market.
He has already pleaded guilty to charges of fraud and forgery in connection with unauthorised trades that Sumitomo says amounted to $2.6 billion in losses by the time he was fired.
Despite the guilty plea, his defence lawyers have said they hope to achieve a light sentence by demonstrating that lax checks and controls at Sumitomo were partly to blame for the huge loss.
